title: The Cheapest Route Across a Table of Costs

concept.title: The cheapest way to a cell is the cost of the cell plus the cheaper of two neighbours
body: A table of numbers is given; entering a cell costs the number written in it (the start cell too). Starting in the top left cell, you move **right or down** until you reach the bottom right cell. What is the smallest total cost of a route? For the table `1 3 1 / 1 5 1 / 4 2 1` the best route 1 -> 3 -> 1 -> 1 -> 1 costs 7.

Let `best(i, j)` be the smallest cost of a route that ends in the cell `(i, j)`. The route came from above or from the left, so we take the **cheaper** of the two and add the cost of the cell: **`best(i, j) = cost(i, j) + min(best(i - 1, j), best(i, j - 1))`**. In the first row only the left neighbour exists, in the first column only the upper one, and `best(0, 0) = cost(0, 0)`.

body.code:
best = [0] * w
for i in range(h):
    for j in range(w):
        if i == 0 and j == 0:  best[j] = cost[0][0]
        elif i == 0:           best[j] = best[j - 1] + cost[i][j]
        elif j == 0:           best[j] = best[j] + cost[i][j]
        else:                  best[j] = min(best[j], best[j - 1]) + cost[i][j]
print(best[w - 1])

body: This is the walled-grid counting problem with the sum replaced by a minimum. One row of the table is enough (`best[j]` still holds the value from the row above until we overwrite it). The time is O(h * w) and the memory O(w). Note that going only right and down is what makes this simple: a route never returns to a cell.

statement: A table with `h` rows and `w` columns holds a cost in each cell. Starting in the top left cell you move one cell right or down at a time until you reach the bottom right cell; the cost of a route is the sum of the numbers in all the cells it visits (including both ends). Print the smallest possible cost.
inputFormat: The first line has `h` and `w`: the number of rows and columns.
Each of the next `h` lines has `w` numbers: one row of the table.
hints: Let best(i, j) be the smallest cost to arrive in the cell (i, j).
You came from above or from the left; take the smaller value and add the cost of the cell.
The first row and the first column have only one neighbour.

starter.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

h, w = map(int, input().split())
cost = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(h)]

# Your code here

explanation: best(i, j) = cost(i, j) + min(best(i - 1, j), best(i, j - 1)) with the border cells having one neighbour; one row of the table is kept, and the value of the last cell is the answer.
